claims.text: A reactive nitrogen environment during Cr deposition will incorporate nitrogen near the Cr/Zr-alloy interface.
The incorporated nitrogen will react with chromium to form a thin CrN interlayer.
The resulting CrN interlayer will be continuous, uniform, and nanometrically thin.
A CrN interlayer reduces atomic mobility across the Cr/Zr-alloy interface.
The CrN interlayer retards high-temperature interdiffusion of Cr and Zr.
The CrN interlayer will not impede protective oxidation behavior in subcritical water or high-temperature steam.
The CrN barrier will help preserve coating integrity under normal-operation and accident-relevant conditions.
Relative to an unmodified elemental Cr coating, the modified coating will exhibit lower Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to the baseline, the modified coating will exhibit less cracking or delamination.
Relative to the baseline, the modified coating will sustain or improve oxidation protection.
The intervention will enhance overall coating durability in both high-temperature steam and subcritical-water environments.
Approximately 300°C is representative of the proposed normal subcritical-water test regime.
Steam exposure at approximately 800°C for one to two hours is representative of the proposed accident-relevant transient regime.
An approximately 1000-hour subcritical-water exposure is within the claimed applicability boundary.
Nitrogen flow, substrate temperature, and deposition bias can affect reactive-nitrogen coating deposition and therefore require optimization.
Cross-interface EDS profiling can be used to assess elemental diffusion gradients and interfacial mixing.
XRD and TEM can confirm whether the intended CrN phase formed and remained stable after exposure.
